title: Some thoughts from a 3D artist.
author: Ok_Feedback4200
selftext:
**What's this post about:**

* My experience trying to create a game using Claude Opus/Fable
* My thoughts and tips on how to do better 3D work with AI

**Quickly about me**: I've been a motion designer/animator/3d artist for 10+ years. I work with various brand and clients. I have experience in preparing 3D for realtime engines but I never worked in the game industry. While early years of AI slop was depressing, now I'm much more optimistic about it. I feel excited about doing design work again while at the same time looking for new workflows and tools that I can build for myself to produce more and better work.  
  
**Regarding slop engines**, I enjoyed playing with Midjourney for a month when it came out. Now I admit sometimes I open it, but honestly, I always treated it more like browsing behance or dribbble. Just instead of searching, I prompt for the inspiration I'm looking for... However, 3 years in, and I feel that these generative slop engines will forever remain that - slop engines. It's dissapointing that MJ is still as inconsistant as it was 3 years ago.

So, now for the part you're probably interested in.. I've been playing with Claude Max for 3 weeks now. I got so hooked I had to get 3x Ultra accounts (extra usage is a complete scam). I tried modeling, texturing, animating, and started developing 3 games, 1 of which was just an early test and is scratched already. 2nd will be a long term spore-like project. This one I'm mainly interested because of the systems that make these creatures and then animate them too. I want to see how far I can get that system with my 3D knowledge.. Because in game like that, you don't model or animate characters.. They have to be made by a system. Anyways.. And a 3rd game I'm working now is a cute little game that I do plan to launch in 1-2 years on both mobile and PC.

**Modeling**... It can be pretty great. But don't except one prompt models to look good. The most obvious thing is to install Blender and MCP server on it, then connect Claude to it. It's free and it works quite good. Personally, I use houdini because there I can keep everything fully procedural, but if I didn't, I'd go with Blender. It helps to start with a concept image. Then a detailed plan on how this is going to be made (fable). Then ask to model it without any textures. Then you have to open it in wireframe mode and inspect it, give feedback. Once you are happy - tell it to save this asset as a reference point for style and quality so it can start producing other assets that will fit the theme.

**Texturing**... This part of 3D was always annoying to me so I'm happy to say that AI is really good at it. UVs - you should educate yourself to know how good UVs look and what rules they must follow in game engines, but as far as the actual work, AI will do it for you. Regarding textures themselves, I personally use substance designer - it's industry standard for creating materials procedurally. But honestly, I'm sure claude can do it with his own tools too. I'd still start with plain 3d models though, and keep texturing for later. 

**Animation**... This is where things get interesting. Check out Kimodo and how to install it locally offline. You'll be able to prompt human animations and run it on your GPU. I wasn't expecting it to work as good as it does. Cascadeur could be an amazing app anyone can learn who's serious about AAA level of character animation (this software is really easy and intuitive to use, it's completely different from traiditional way of working with 3D character animations.. Spoiler alert: big part of the workflow inside it can also be automated by Claude. So I do believe this is the ultimate choice for the serious game devs who want to have great quality character animations in their game.. When it  comes to animating everything else - Claude can be quite amazing. Sure, it heavily depends on how complex the tasks are, but in general, abstract animations are now very easy to prompt and direct. However, this is also where the 'animators eye' comes into play, something that has to be trained in years. So I'm genuinely curious to see non animators work on their 3D animations and seeing them decide what looks good or bad in their opinion..

**UI/UX**. Claude sucks ass at it. But.. if you ask it to research again and again from scratch, it might give you decent UX experience.. But I do think that his area is super important for every AI game dev to focus now. Because AI won't give you good UI, and UI plays huge role in the games..

**Design**... Here, AI sucks too. You could say that slop engines like Midjourney can produce good designs, because they are trained on actual artwork and their output is a scramble of them, so sometimes it does produce what form first sight could look like an amazing design. Of course, till you start looking into details.. One more important thought I'll leave you with... New design styles are emerging and getting popular. 'Bad design' is one of them. If you end up creating art on your own, in your own style, even if it looks like from the 90s, if it captures the vibe correctly, you can capture huge audiences with it.

**Lastly, and most importantly, how I think everyone should be using AI while creating stuff like games, animations, designs, etc:**  
**Work for the systems. Not for the first output you get.**

You want to start using AI to model stuff for you game? Great, create a system which AI will follow each time so all your assets come out looking the same like they belong together. You improve your system - all your output improves too.

And don't be afraid to think outside the box. When you have Claude Max, it can be all you need. You can very quickly and easily create specialized web based apps that could serve you as your own animation/texturing/design/etc tool. Don't just ask AI to do everything for you. Ask it to create tools specifically made for you.. Research how these tools work, think what skills you have and how you'd like to work, and create your own workflows. There are no more rules to follow when it comes to creating stuff.
